title: Argent Harbor hermetic delivery + kernel warmup benchmark sync

Agreed next steps include handing over packaging checklist, sample signed manifest, and running a 2-hour warmup benchmark in staging with telemetry collection.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Raj Singh (Argent Harbor - DevOps), Lina Morales (Argent Harbor - Security), Tom Becker (Argent Harbor - ML Infra)

Summary: quick sync on hermetic delivery approach for air-gapped stacks, driver signing, offline licensing, and a KV cache warmup benchmark.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Alright folks, thanks for carving out time. Today's objective is to align on the hermetic delivery path — the physical package, the signed manifest, and the warmup / benchmark plan so your runtime doesn't hit cold-KV penalties in production.
[00:18] Raj Singh: Yeah thanks, Alex. We've got strict IT policy here, host kernels are locked down and anything that touches module signing needs CISO sign-off, so that's the biggest gating factor.
[00:27] Maya Patel: Understood, Raj. We'll show two options: (1) use vendor-signed kernel modules that fit your mksign policy, or (2) run in-container user-space runtime that avoids external kernel modules. Both have tradeoffs around NVidia driver stacks and perf.
[00:42] Lina Morales: Can you clarify 'vendor-signed'? Our policy requires internal key signing for any kernel module. We can't accept third party keys in prod.
[00:52] Maya Patel: Right, so we can provide a build of the GPU kernel shim that you can sign internally — we'll include the source, build scripts, and a reproducible recipe. The package will include a GPG-signed manifest listing checksums for each artifact.
[01:06] Tom Becker: How big are the artifacts? We're trying to plan logistics for the air transfer.
[01:11] Alex Chen: Typical model artifacts for the medium LLM we're recommending are about 12-18 GB compressed, runtime tarball ~1.2 GB, driver artifacts ~200-400 MB depending on variant. Also we'll provide a binary delta for future patches to reduce transfer sizes.
[01:27] Raj Singh: Ok so physical transfer via encrypted drive. On policy we need chain-of-custody: who touches the drive, when, checksum recorded.
[01:35] Maya Patel: We'll provide a signed manifest (GPG) and a SHA-256 checksum file. The manifest includes artifact name, size, checksum, and GPG signature. Recommendation: verify signature against the included root key and then re-sign with your internal key before installation.
[01:52] Lina Morales: For offline license activation — how does the license handshake work without outbound connectivity?
[01:58] Alex Chen: Offline activation uses a signed license token file that your ops team exchanges with the Redwood licensing console through an offline provisioning step. Process: request -> get signed license blob -> transfer to air-gapped environment -> run local activation CLI which validates the signature and writes a license to the local key store. No phone-home required after the blob is signed.
[02:21] Raj Singh: Who signs the license blob? Can we audit the signature and key rotation?
[02:25] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood uses a short-lived signing key per customer shipment. We'll provide the public verification key and an audit trail CSV showing request ID, signed timestamp, and fingerprint. We can also support HSM-backed signing on our side if you need more guarantees.
[02:40] Tom Becker: On the runtime side, we need to benchmark warmup of the KV cache. Cold-start latency on our previous self-host was brutal. What's your recommended approach?
[02:48] Maya Patel: Two-phase warmup: (A) prefix pre-warm using representative prompts to populate prefix cache and KV entries, (B) continuous steady-state warmup using synthetic traffic to stabilize batching and token distribution. For hermetic runs we suggest using a 2-hour pre-warm with burst phases to exercise eviction windows.
[03:07] Raj Singh: That sounds heavy. Will that saturate GPU memory?
[03:11] Maya Patel: We size the workload by model and sequence length. Example: for a 13B quantized model with 32k KV budget, pre-warm will use incremental prefixes to avoid blowing memory. We'll provide a script that increments the active prefix set and monitors OOM.
[03:26] Lina Morales: What telemetry travels out of the air-gapped environment during the benchmark? We can't allow logs to leave.
[03:31] Alex Chen: All telemetry is optional. For the on-prem bench, we provide a telemetry agent that writes to a local Grafana/Prometheus stack. If you want us to analyze results, you can sanitize and transfer the tarball of metrics; otherwise we'll give you the dashboard templates and alert rules.
[03:50] Tom Becker: Great. Let's talk numbers — target SLO is 50ms p95 for single-turn generation at 16-token lengths. Is that realistic in hermetic mode?
[03:59] Maya Patel: With quantization and pinned KV cache, p95 of 40-60ms is achievable on A100-class or equivalent if you tune batch sizes and kernel selection. The tricky part is continuous batching: small bursts reduce batching efficiency, so we tune max_batch and latency headroom.
[04:17] Raj Singh: We have mixed hardware — some 80GB A100s and a couple of older 40GB cards. Will the runtime support heterogeneous pools without internet?
[04:26] Maya Patel: Yes — runtime supports model variants per device type. We'll use the same deployment manifest but tag devices locally. In air-gapped mode the router uses static policies in the config rather than live cloud-based routing.
[04:38] Alex Chen: Also note that quantization profile matters. We'll recommend int8 profile for 40GB cards and int4/8 mix for 80GB to optimize KV storage vs compute. We'll include the recommended quant config files in the package.
[04:53] Tom Becker: Any caveats on driver versions? We've had kernel module breakage after driver upgrades.
[04:59] Maya Patel: Common issue. We test against longterm kernels you provide. For NVIDIA stacks, we support driver families 525.x and 535.x on our runtime builds; we include DKMS recipes but because your hosts are locked, we recommend the signed-module approach: you build & sign the module with your internal key using mokutil or internal signing, then load it. We also supply an option to run the runtime in user-space mode that avoids kernel shims but comes with a small perf penalty.
[05:30] Raj Singh: Could you repeat the user-space option tradeoff?
[05:33] Maya Patel: Sure — user-space runtime uses standard GPU compute via vendor driver without extra kernel modules. It simplifies policy but we lose some low-level queue optimizations and NVLink special paths, so expect ~8-12% higher latency on tail in some workloads.
[05:48] Lina Morales: On manifest signing — can you provide a sample manifest and a verification checklist?
[05:52] Alex Chen: Yes, will share sample-manifest.gpg and a step-by-step checklist. We'll also include a minimal verification script that checks GPG signatures and SHA-256 checksums.
[06:03] Tom Becker: During the warmup, how do you avoid polluting the cache with synthetic tokens that don't match production distribution?
[06:09] Maya Patel: Two tactics: (1) use representative prompt corpus derived from your logs (sanitized) — we provided a prompt-scrub template; (2) schedule diversity windows that insert longer tail prompts periodically to prime KV eviction behavior.
[06:24] Raj Singh: For the physical transport, we need to sign a chain-of-custody form. Does Redwood have a recommended template?
[06:30] Alex Chen: Yes — we'll attach a chain-of-custody template. It includes: shipper, recipient, checksummed manifest, time stamps, and signature fields. Ideally the drive is encrypted with LUKS and the passphrase transmitted via separate channel to the on-site custodian.
[06:45] Lina Morales: Is the license blob tied to hardware fingerprint? We want to ensure the license cannot be used on other hosts.
[06:51] Alex Chen: It can be. We can bind a license to host UUIDs or MACs, or to an HSM key in the environment. For more flexibility we issue a grace token plus a hardware-bound activation for production.
[07:04] Tom Becker: Let's sprint through the benchmark plan specifics — what's the script flow?
[07:08] Maya Patel: High level: (1) install runtime and signed modules, (2) deploy model artifacts from the signed manifest, (3) run baseline microbench (single request latency), (4) run 2-hour warmup with ramp phases: 0-15m ramp, 15-60m steady high, 60-90m diversity bursts, 90-120m cool-down; (5) collect metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, memcpy stalls, kv-hit/miss, batch sizes, and OOM events.
[07:35] Raj Singh: For the KV metrics — what's the format?
[07:38] Maya Patel: We emit KV hits/misses per minute and also provide a KV heatmap per-token position so you can see eviction patterns. The metric names will be prometheus-style: redwood_kv_hits_total, redwood_kv_misses_total, redwood_batch_size_avg.
[07:52] Alex Chen: We'll also include a small helper that converts local Prometheus snapshots into an exportable tarball for offline review.
[07:58] Tom Becker: About fallback policies — if a host loses a signed module or fails validation can the workload shift to another node without internet?
[08:06] Maya Patel: Yes — the orchestrator uses local static policies and can fail over to alternate devices in the pool. If everything for that pool fails, you can configure a local 'degraded' policy that reduces concurrency and keeps latency SLOs by shedding heavy requests.
[08:19] Raj Singh: Security question: do the runtime logs include prompt text? That would be a blocker for us.
[08:24] Lina Morales: We can't allow prompt text in logs.
[08:26] Maya Patel: By default logs redact prompt text. You can toggle collection of full prompts but that requires explicit SSO-admin enable and is off for hermetic shipments. The local telemetry will only record hashes and token counts unless you opt-in.
[08:40] Alex Chen: Quick check — are there any external compliance artifacts you need that we haven't covered? SOC2, ISO, signed SLA?
[08:47] Lina Morales: We need SOC2 attestation and the signed SLA. Also a data processing addendum that covers on-prem telemetry handling.
[08:55] Alex Chen: We'll attach the SOC2 letter and DPA template.
[08:59] Raj Singh: Good. A couple of on-the-ground ops questions: (1) do you support DKMS so we can rebuild kernel modules across distro kernels? (2) any recommended kernel parameters for hugepages or NUMA?
[09:09] Maya Patel: Yes DKMS scripts are included. We recommend tuning hugepages for large-model KV to reduce page faults and set vm.swappiness low. For NUMA, pin GPUs and CPU threads to the same NUMA domain and use our affinity script to avoid cross NUMA traffic. We'll include example systemd and tuned profiles.
[09:28] Tom Becker: If during warmup we see a high p99 tail at 300-400ms, what immediate mitigations should we try?
[09:34] Maya Patel: Quick triage: check for OOM/kernels churn, validate batch sizes (reduce max_batch to avoid head-of-line blocking), ensure KV cache warmup is complete (run the prefix pre-warm script), and check driver interrupts or PCIe errors. We'll share a triage checklist.
[09:52] Alex Chen: Let's capture concrete deliverables. Maya, you'll share the packaging checklist, sample manifest, DKMS recipe, quant config and benchmark scripts. Raj will provide kernel list and secure-share access. Tom will run the warmup in staging and upload metrics.
[10:05] Raj Singh: Yep I can do that. Lina will review security artifacts once we have the sample manifest.
[10:12] Lina Morales: One more note: we require that any binary install steps be reproducible so our security team can rebuild if needed.
[10:19] Maya Patel: We'll include full build instructions and CI reproducible hashes for runtime and kernel module builds.
[10:26] Alex Chen: Perfect. Any other blockers before we wrap?
[10:29] Raj Singh: None from my side.
[10:31] Tom Becker: All good.
[10:33] Lina Morales: Fine here.
[10:34] Alex Chen: Ok thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts by Monday. Recap of next steps
